client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time my family gets together, I just can't seem to enjoy it — all I can think about is that she's not there, and it kind of ruins everything for me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and being here — even when part of you isn't sure it will help, showing up takes real courage. The grief you're carrying comes through so clearly, and it makes complete sense that family gatherings feel hollow right now, because they're also reminders of the space she used to fill. What you're experiencing isn't something "ruining" things for you — it's actually a reflection of how deeply you loved her, and that's something we can gently work through together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure reframing it as "a reflection of love" really makes it feel any better in the moment. Like, when I'm sitting at the dinner table and her chair is just... empty, knowing I loved her doesn't stop the ache from hitting me like a wall. I guess I'm just wondering if talking about it is actually going to make those moments hurt less, or if I'm just going to keep reliving them.
therapist: You're absolutely right to push back on that — reframing doesn't make the ache disappear, and I don't want to offer you words that feel hollow when the pain is that immediate and physical. I notice there's something almost urgent in how you're expressing this, like you really need to know this won't just be an exercise in talking circles around the hurt. The honest answer is that we're not here to make you stop feeling it — we're here to help you carry it in a way that doesn't steal every future moment at that table from you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually lands a little differently than I expected — "carry it" rather than "get over it" feels more honest somehow. But I guess my fear is that I'll be carrying it forever and it'll just keep getting heavier, not lighter. Like, what does that even look like in practice, because right now I can't picture sitting at that table and feeling anything other than completely gutted.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — there's a real tension in your voice, like part of you is reaching for hope but another part is bracing for disappointment, and that makes complete sense one month in. Grief doesn't actually get heavier with time for most people; what changes is that you slowly build more capacity around it, so the weight becomes a smaller proportion of what you're able to hold — but I hear you that right now that's almost impossible to imagine. What might help is starting very small: not picturing the whole dinner, but just one tiny moment at that table where something — a smell, a joke, a dish she loved — might connect you to her rather than just remind you of her absence.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea of finding a connecting moment instead of just feeling the absence is... interesting, I guess, but I'm not sure I can just switch gears like that in the middle of feeling overwhelmed. Like, my aunt made my grandmother's apple cake last week and instead of feeling connected to her, I just started crying in the bathroom because it made everything more real, not less. I don't know if I'm doing grief wrong or if that kind of thing just isn't going to work for me the way you're describing.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, like you're carefully holding something fragile — tells me that moment with the apple cake really stayed with you, and I want to say clearly: you are not doing grief wrong. Crying in the bathroom *is* a connecting moment, even though it didn't feel like one — your body was responding to love made tangible in that cake, and that's not a failure of the process, that's the process. We don't need to aim for moments that feel peaceful or healing right away; sometimes the connection just looks like tears, and that counts too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hadn't thought about it that way — that the crying was actually me connecting to her, not just falling apart. But I guess part of me still feels embarrassed about it, like I should be holding it together better around my family instead of sneaking off to the bathroom. I don't know how to just let myself have those moments without feeling like I'm burdening everyone or making the gathering harder for them too.
therapist: There's something tender in the way you're saying this — soft and careful, like you're almost apologizing for having feelings at all — and I want to gently challenge the thought that your grief is a burden to others. It's worth asking: has anyone in your family actually told you your tears made things harder, or is that a story you're telling yourself to protect them, perhaps at the cost of your own permission to grieve? More often than not, people who love each other find it quietly relieving to see someone else feeling what they're also trying to hold alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: No, nobody's actually said that to me directly — I think I've just been assuming it because my mom and my uncle seem to be holding it together so well on the outside. But now that you're asking, I wonder if they're doing the same thing I am, just... hiding in different rooms. It's a little unsettling to consider that we might all be grieving alone in the same house without anyone actually reaching toward each other.
therapist: The way you just said that — very quietly, almost like the realization was fragile and you didn't want to break it — tells me this landed somewhere important for you. You've just shifted from "I'm burdening my family" to "we might all be carrying this alone together," and that's a significant crack in a belief that's been keeping you isolated in your own grief. I wonder what it might feel like to be the one who reaches first — not to fix anyone's pain, but just to let someone in your family know they don't have to hide in a different room.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: The idea of reaching out first is both appealing and terrifying, because what if I bring it up and my mom just shuts down or changes the subject — then I'd feel even more alone than before. I think I've been protecting myself from that possibility by just assuming everyone wants to keep things surface-level at gatherings. I don't really know how you even start that kind of conversation without it feeling forced or like you're making a big dramatic announcement.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quick and soft, like the words are tumbling out faster than you can catch them — tells me this feels both urgent and vulnerable, and I want to name that the fear you're describing is completely valid. But notice what you just did: you've been assuming everyone wants to stay surface-level, and yet earlier you couldn't imagine your aunt made that apple cake without thinking of your grandmother too — so the evidence already suggests the people around you are closer to the surface than they're letting on. It doesn't have to be a big announcement; sometimes it starts as small as saying to your mom, "I really miss her today," and just seeing what she does with that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: "I really miss her today" — that's so simple it almost feels too small for how big the feeling is, but maybe that's actually what makes it less scary to try. I guess my worry is that I'll say it and then just completely lose it, and then instead of a small moment it turns into me being a mess and my mom not knowing how to handle it. I don't have great evidence that she's good at sitting with emotions — she's always been more of a "let's keep busy and move forward" kind of person.
therapist: Your voice is soft but moving quickly, like part of you is already rehearsing how it might go wrong — and I want to acknowledge that your concern about your mom isn't unfounded, you know her better than anyone. But here's something worth sitting with: even if she does deflect or keep busy, that wouldn't mean your grief was too much or wrong — it would just mean she has her own way of coping, and that's about her limits, not your worth. And honestly, "completely losing it" in front of your mom might be less about falling apart and more about finally letting someone else witness what you've been carrying alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe — that it's about her limits and not my worth — is something I really want to believe, but I'm not sure I fully do yet. There's still this voice in my head that says if she deflects, it'll confirm some fear I have that even the people closest to me can't really hold space for how I feel. I think that's maybe a bigger thing underneath all of this, and it's a little scary to realize it right now.
therapist: The way you just said that — high and fast, like the words were almost outrunning you — tells me this realization caught you off guard, and I want to honor how brave it is to name it out loud. What you've just uncovered isn't a small thing: underneath the grief, there's a deeper fear that you're too much to be held, and that fear likely didn't start with your grandmother's passing. That's exactly the kind of thing worth exploring gently together, because you deserve to find out whether that voice is telling you the truth — or whether it's a story that's been protecting you at a very high cost.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: You're probably right that it didn't start with losing her, but I'm not sure I'm ready to go digging into all of that today — it feels like I came in with one wound and now there might be something much older underneath it. I guess I'm a little worried that if we pull on that thread, it's going to unravel more than I can handle right now. Can we maybe just stay with the grief for a while longer before we go somewhere that feels even bigger?
therapist: Absolutely — and the fact that you could name that boundary and ask for what you need is itself something worth noticing, because it means you're already trusting yourself more than that fear gives you credit for. We can stay right here with your grandmother, with the apple cake, with the empty chair, for as long as that's where you need to be. The older thread will still be there when and if you're ever ready, and nothing has to be unraveled before you feel safe enough to hold it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
